description: How armour, monuments and relief sculpture depicted and idealised war — from the Lenormant relief to Trajan's Column.
content_html:
Reading War Through Objects and Monuments

The ancient world did not record war only in words. Armour, weapons, coins, sculptural reliefs and triumphal arches were all part of how war was presented, commemorated and made meaningful. These material culture of war tells us things literary sources cannot: how soldiers actually looked, how battles felt to those watching a monument built in their city, and — crucially — how victory was turned into a lasting statement of power. This lesson draws together the main prescribed visual and material sources for ancient warfare.

Helmets, Armour and Identity

Individual pieces of armour are among the most personal of all military artefacts. The Corinthian helmet is the most iconic type associated with Greek hoplite warfare. The prescribed Corinthian helmet in the British Museum (1824, 0407.32), dedicated to Zeus at Olympia around 460 BC, is made of hammered bronze, shaped to cover the entire head and face except for a narrow T-shaped opening for the eyes and mouth. The front was decorated with a sharp nasal guard, and in use a crest of horsehair would have been fitted to the top. The decoration on many Corinthian helmets — serpents, owls, Gorgon faces — was intended both to terrify the enemy and to invoke divine protection.

That this particular helmet was dedicated at Olympia is significant. Victorious athletes and generals dedicated trophies and weapons at major sanctuaries as acts of thanksgiving to the gods. A helmet hung in the sanctuary of Zeus was simultaneously a religious offering and a public advertisement of military success. The object thus functioned in two registers: as a piece of military equipment and as a religious artefact. This dual function is typical of Greek material culture — the boundary between the military and the sacred was always porous.

Key Fact

The Corinthian helmet in the British Museum (1824, 0407.32) dates to around 460 BC and was dedicated to Zeus at Olympia. It is made of hammered bronze with a T-shaped face opening. Its dedication at a sanctuary shows how Greeks combined military success with religious thanksgiving.

The Lenormant Trireme Relief

The Lenormant Trireme relief is a fragment of carved marble originally from the Acropolis at Athens, dating to around 410 BC. The relief shows the side view of a trireme in motion: the three banks of oarsmen are visible in a staggered arrangement, with the oars protruding outwards at different angles. The crew’s physical effort is suggested by the angle and position of the figures, and a helmsman is visible at the stern. The level of detail in the carving gives us direct evidence for how the trireme was crewed and how its three-bank rowing system worked.

The relief is also useful for understanding naval battle tactics. The trireme’s primary weapon was its bronze-sheathed ram at the waterline. In a battle like Salamis (480 BC), Athenian triremes rowed at speed towards enemy vessels and tried to shear off their oars or punch through their hull with the ram. The Lenormant relief, showing the rowers’ arrangement, helps us understand why speed and coordination were so critical: all three banks of rowers had to stroke in precise rhythm, guided by the flute-player and the helmsman, to generate the burst of speed needed for an effective ramming run.

The Lenormant relief is a fragment — it shows only a portion of one side of one ship. It does not show the full crew in action, the complete three-bank arrangement in cross-section, or the conditions below deck. Scholars have debated for decades exactly how many rowers a trireme carried (the standard figure is 170) and precisely how the three banks were arranged at the sides of the hull. The relief provides a crucial visual snapshot but cannot settle all the questions archaeologists and historians still have about trireme design. This is a reminder of a broader truth: all material sources are fragmentary, and we must be honest about what they can and cannot establish.

Battle Scenes in Greek Sculpture

Greek sculptors regularly depicted warfare on temple friezes and pediments. The South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis, now in the British Museum, shows Greeks fighting Persians in a swirling scene of battle. The carving is in high relief — figures project dramatically from the background, their limbs intertwined in combat. A fallen Persian warrior lies beneath an Athenian who strides over him. The composition celebrates Athenian victory, with Greek figures shown as larger and more dynamic than their opponents. The red-figure kylix by the Triptolemos Painter showing a Persian and a Greek fighting is a complementary source — painted pottery gave the same narrative a domestic scale, bringing images of victory into private homes.

Key Fact

Three prescribed material sources relate to Greek warfare: the South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike (marble, British Museum — Greeks fighting Persians); the Lenormant Trireme relief (marble, Acropolis — trireme crew at the oars); the Triptolemos Painter kylix (red-figure pot — Persian and Greek in single combat). Each medium — temple relief, architectural fragment, painted vase — presented war to different audiences.

Roman War Monuments and Commemoration

Rome systematised the commemoration of war on a massive public scale. Trajan’s Column, discussed in an earlier lesson, is the most famous example: a 30-metre marble column with a continuous spiral relief recording both Dacian campaigns in over 150 scenes. The Arch of Trajan at Benevento is decorated with relief panels showing the emperor in his dual role as warrior and benefactor. The relief commemorating the battle of Actium in the Vatican Museum offers a sculptural record of that decisive naval battle, depicting ships and combat in a style calculated to glorify Octavian’s victory.

Coins are among the most widely distributed material sources for Roman warfare. The Mark Antony Legionary denarius (minted approximately 32 BC, example in the British Museum BMC 197) has a warship with banners on one face and an eagle between two military standards on the other. This coin was literally struck to pay soldiers before the battle of Actium: it was a wage payment that also served as propaganda, advertising Antony’s fleet and his military strength. The coin type tells us about the relationship between payment, loyalty and military identity in the Roman world — a legionary holding this coin was being told, in miniature, that he was part of a powerful armed force with divine symbols on its side.

Both Greek and Roman visual sources idealise war rather than record it neutrally. Greek temple friezes show Athenians as powerful, upright and victorious over crumpling Persians — this is a political statement, not a documentary record. Roman monuments go further: Trajan’s Column never shows Roman soldiers committing atrocities, looting civilians or running away. The defeated Dacians are shown as brave enemies to make the conquest more impressive, and Trajan himself is always central and commanding. Both traditions use selectivity to project the values their societies most wanted to celebrate — courage, discipline, divine favour and civic virtue. Students who treat these sources as straightforward records will miss half the information they contain.
exam_tip_html: Source analysis is at the heart of this topic. When you are given a visual source in the exam, identify: (1) what the object is and its medium (marble relief, bronze statuette, red-figure pot, coin); (2) specific details you can see or know about it; (3) what those details reveal about warfare or military values; (4) what the source cannot tell us or how it may be selective or biased. A response that only describes what the object looks like, without moving to analysis and evaluation, will score in the lower bands. Aim to use the phrase “this reveals” or “this suggests” to push yourself from description to analysis.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Key prescribed material sources for Greek warfare include the Corinthian helmet dedicated at Olympia (British Museum), the Lenormant Trireme relief (showing trireme crew), the South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike (Greeks vs Persians), and the Triptolemos Painter kylix; each presents war to a different audience and in a different medium.
  • Roman sources — Trajan’s Column, the Arch of Trajan at Benevento, the Actium relief, and the Mark Antony Legionary denarius — systematically glorified Roman military victories and the emperors who won them.
  • All these sources are selective: they present idealised versions of war and must be evaluated critically — what they show, what they choose not to show, and for what audience and purpose they were created.

practice_questions.text: Name one prescribed visual source that provides evidence for naval warfare in ancient Greece.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: the Lenormant Trireme relief (Acropolis relief); the red-figure kylix of a Persian and Greek fighting by the Triptolemos Painter (accept either); the South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Corinthian helmet dedicated at Olympia (British Museum 1824, 0407.32) and explain what it reveals about Greek military and religious practice.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point up to three: the helmet is made of hammered bronze; it covers the entire head and face except for a T-shaped opening for eyes and mouth; it was made around 460 BC; it was dedicated to Zeus at Olympia as a religious offering after a military success; this shows that Greeks combined military victory with religious thanksgiving; dedicating weapons at sanctuaries was a way of publicly advertising military achievement.

practice_questions.text:
Look at this description of a prescribed Greek material source: a fragment of carved marble, approximately 50 cm in length, showing the side view of a large rowing vessel. Three staggered rows of oarsmen are visible, each row set slightly higher than the one below. The oars project outward at different angles, suggesting the ship is in motion. A helmsman figure is faintly visible at one end. The fragment was found on the Acropolis at Athens.

What does this source tell us about naval warfare in ancient Greece? Use specific details from the source in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis linking specific features (three staggered banks of rowers, oars at angles, helmsman position) to wider knowledge of trireme design and tactics (ramming speed requiring coordinated rowing, the role of the helmsman, the arrangement needed for three-bank rowing). The response also evaluates the source's limitations: it is a fragment, it does not show the full ship in cross-section, it shows the ship at rest or gentle rowing rather than in the burst of speed needed for ramming. At least two specific details are used analytically.
Secure: Clear use of specific details with accurate supporting knowledge of the trireme. Some evaluative comment.
Developing: General reference to oarsmen and the trireme; limited use of specific details.
Emerging: Minimal engagement; vague knowledge.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Roman monuments were designed to communicate ideas about military power.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point plus 1 mark for development, up to four marks. Points might include: Trajan's Column placed the narrative of conquest at the heart of the city where every Roman could see it; the Arch of Trajan at Benevento was positioned on a major road so that every traveller was reminded of Roman victory; the continuous spiral narrative on Trajan's Column presented the campaigns as a coherent story of Roman greatness; relief sculpture always showed the emperor in commanding positions; coins spread military imagery to every corner of the empire; these monuments associated the emperor with divine favour and military excellence.

practice_questions.text: How useful are the prescribed material sources for understanding what it was actually like to fight in ancient warfare?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced analysis covering the genuine information provided by material sources (equipment visible on the bronze legionary statuette; rowing system visible on the Lenormant Trireme relief; tactics implied by relief carving) against their fundamental limitations (all are official or elite productions; none show fear, fatigue, death or defeat from the combatant's perspective; all idealise). The response argues that material sources tell us a great deal about how war was presented but much less about how it was experienced by ordinary soldiers. Named sources are used precisely.
Secure: Clear discussion of both uses and limitations, with specific reference to named sources.
Developing: Mainly one-sided; either uncritically values material sources or dismisses them.
Emerging: Vague; limited source knowledge; largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: How effectively do the prescribed material sources present the reality of war in the ancient world? Use a range of evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument engaging with a range of prescribed sources (Corinthian helmet, Lenormant Trireme relief, Temple of Athena Nike frieze, Triptolemos Painter kylix, Trajan's Column, Arch of Trajan, Actium relief, Mark Antony denarius) and evaluating what each reveals and conceals. The response argues that all material sources are selective — they present war through the lens of commemoration, propaganda or religious offering rather than lived experience — but that together they reveal military equipment, tactics, logistics and values with considerable precision. The response considers the difference between Greek and Roman approaches to commemorating war. A supported judgement is reached.
Secure: A clear argument engaging with at least four named sources, weighing their uses and limitations. A supported conclusion.
Developing: Covers two or three sources; limited balance or development.
Emerging: Simple points; largely descriptive; few named sources.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the Lenormant Trireme relief show?
options: A Greek soldier in hoplite armour about to charge
The crew of a trireme at their oars with three staggered banks of rowers
A Roman general receiving the surrender of a Dacian king
A naval battle scene with ships ramming each other

knowledge_checks.q: The Corinthian helmet in the British Museum (1824, 0407.32) was dedicated at which sanctuary?
options: The Temple of Apollo at Delphi
The sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia

knowledge_checks.q: The Mark Antony Legionary denarius was minted around 32 BC and shows a warship on one side and an _____ between two standards on the other.
The South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike shows _____ fighting Persians in a scene celebrating Athenian victory.
Match each material source to the type of evidence it provides:
right: A continuous spiral narrative recording two military campaigns
A rowing vessel showing three staggered banks of oarsmen
A piece of actual armour dedicated at a sanctuary after victory

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Lenormant Trireme relief, and where was it found?
flashcard_questions.a: A marble fragment from the Acropolis at Athens showing a trireme crew at their oars.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Lenormant Trireme relief show about how the trireme was crewed?
flashcard_questions.a: Three staggered banks of rowers, with a helmsman at the stern guiding the vessel.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of helmet is in the British Museum (1824, 0407.32) and when was it made?
flashcard_questions.a: A Corinthian bronze helmet, made around 460 BC.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was the Corinthian helmet dedicated at Olympia rather than kept as a trophy?
flashcard_questions.a: It was a religious offering to Zeus, combining military success with thanksgiving to the gods.

flashcard_questions.q: What scene does the South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike depict?
flashcard_questions.a: Greeks fighting Persians, celebrating Athenian military victory.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Triptolemos Painter kylix, and what does it show?
flashcard_questions.a: A red-figure pot showing a Persian and a Greek in single combat.

flashcard_questions.q: What two images appear on the Mark Antony Legionary denarius?
flashcard_questions.a: A warship with banners on one side; an eagle between two military standards on the other.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main limitation of Trajan's Column as a source for Roman warfare?
flashcard_questions.a: It is imperial propaganda; it omits Roman failures, atrocities and the suffering of civilians.

flashcard_questions.q: What is 'material culture' in the context of classical studies?
flashcard_questions.a: The physical objects, art and architecture through which a society expresses and records its values.

flashcard_questions.q: In what way was the Corinthian helmet a 'dual function' artefact?
flashcard_questions.a: It served as military equipment in battle and as a religious offering and public trophy in peacetime.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the kylix mean as an object type?
flashcard_questions.a: A red-figure Greek drinking cup decorated with narrative scenes against a black background.

flashcard_questions.q: Which prescribed source is a relief commemorating the battle of Actium, and where is it held?
flashcard_questions.a: The relief commemorating Actium is in the Vatican Museum.

glossary_terms.definition: The physical objects, art and architecture through which a society expresses, records and transmits its experiences and values; in classical studies, this includes weapons, coins, sculpture and monuments.
A type of Greek helmet with a protective guard covering the cheeks and nasal, leaving only a narrow T-shaped opening; widely used from the seventh to fifth century BC.
A marble relief from the Acropolis of Athens showing the crew of a trireme warship at their oars; one of the best material sources for understanding how the trireme was operated.
A Greek painted drinking cup decorated with figures left in the natural red colour of the clay against a black-painted background; used widely for narrative scenes of myth and everyday life.
